Misfortune means bad luck, or a specific event caused by bad luck that brings difficulty, pain, or loss to someone.
The Two Ways It Is Used

1. As a general state (bad luck in general)
Here, misfortune refers to the condition of things going badly — not because of what you did, but because circumstances simply did not go in your favour.

"She experienced great misfortune in her early years."

This means she went through a lot of bad, difficult situations over time.

2. As a specific event (a particular unlucky happening)
Here, misfortune refers to one concrete unfortunate event.

"Losing his job was a misfortune he had not expected."
"The floods were a terrible misfortune for the village."

In this sense, you can say "a misfortune" (one event) or "misfortunes" (several such events).
The Heart of the Word

The most important feeling inside "misfortune" is this: it happened to someone — they didn't bring it on themselves. It carries a sense of undeserved suffering, of circumstances being outside your control.

  • Being born poor → misfortune (you didn't choose it)
  • Losing your house in a flood → misfortune (you couldn't stop it)
  • Losing your savings because of reckless gambling → this is less "misfortune" and more "consequence of a bad choice"

This is why we feel sympathy for someone who has suffered misfortune. The word has a natural compassion built into it.

That said, in everyday use, people sometimes say "misfortune" even when the person's own choices played a role — so it's not a strict rule, just the core flavour of the word.
A Very Common Phrase: "Have the Misfortune of / to"

This phrase means you experienced something unpleasant or unlucky.

"I had the misfortune of sitting next to a very rude passenger on the flight."
"She had the misfortune to arrive just as the argument broke out."

This phrasing is often used in a slightly ironic, calm, understated tone — you're describing something bad in a composed, almost polite way, as if saying, "well, unfortunately, this happened to me."
Tone: Formal and Dignified

"Misfortune" is more formal and literary than simply saying "bad luck." You'll find it in books, serious journalism, formal speech, and careful writing. It sounds weightier and more empathetic.

Compare:

  • "He had bad luck." — informal, casual, everyday
  • "He suffered great misfortune." — formal, more serious, more dignified

Both mean the same thing at the core, but misfortune carries a graver, more respectful tone. It suits situations where something genuinely painful or significant happened.
Plural: Misfortunes

When you say "misfortunes" (plural), you usually mean a series of unfortunate events — multiple bad things piling up.

"Despite all the misfortunes she had faced, she refused to give up."
"That year brought misfortune after misfortune — illness, financial loss, and loneliness."

There's a well-known saying: "Misfortunes never come alone" — meaning that when one bad thing happens, more tend to follow. (You may also know the phrase from the children's book series A Series of Unfortunate Events, which is essentially a series of misfortunes hitting the same family again and again.)
How It Differs from Similar Words

Bad luck — the casual, everyday version of misfortune. Same meaning, less formal.

Disaster / Calamity — much larger and more catastrophic in scale. A flood that destroys a city is a disaster. Missing your train is a misfortune. Misfortune can be personal and small; disasters are usually large.

Tragedy — carries deep emotional pain and usually involves death, permanent loss, or something irreversible. A tragedy is more extreme and emotionally heavier than a misfortune.

Adversity — refers to the difficult conditions a person lives under (poverty, war, hardship), rather than the unlucky event that caused them. Someone faces adversity; they suffer a misfortune. Adversity is about ongoing struggle; misfortune is about the unlucky event itself.

Hardship — focuses on how difficult the conditions are (hunger, poverty, exhaustion), not on the unlucky cause. Misfortune = "something bad happened to you through no fault of your own." Hardship = "life is very hard and demanding."
Words That Naturally Go with Misfortune

These are natural pairings you'll see and hear often:

  • suffer a misfortune — to experience it
  • face misfortune — to be confronted by bad circumstances
  • a great misfortune — a significant one
  • a personal misfortune — something that happened to you specifically
  • a series of misfortunes — several bad things in a row
  • have the misfortune of — to experience something unfortunate (see phrase above)
  • fall into misfortune — to gradually end up in a bad situation
Scale

Misfortune is flexible in how serious it is. It can describe something small and inconvenient or something large and life-changing:

  • Small: "It was a misfortune that we arrived just as it started raining."
  • Large: "Losing his entire family was the greatest misfortune of his life."

The surrounding words (great, terrible, small, minor) usually signal how severe the misfortune is.
In a Nutshell

Misfortune = bad luck, or a specific unlucky event, that causes difficulty or suffering — and which the person did not deserve or could not control.

It is formal in tone, compassionate in feel, flexible in scale (from minor inconveniences to major life-altering events), and can refer both to the general experience of bad luck and to specific unfortunate events.
